title: WHAT GOD LOOKS FOR IN A HUSBAND
paragraphs:
WHAT GOD LOOKS FOR IN A HUSBAND
The Question Every Man Should Fear, Every Woman Should Understand, and Every Christian Should Bring Before the Cross
What if the greatest qualification for being a husband is not what most people spend their lives trying to become?
Not success.
Not wealth.
Not confidence.
Not attractiveness.
Not influence.
Not status.
Not even the ability to provide.
What if heaven looks for something entirely different?
What if the question God asks is not, "Can he build a career?" but, "Can he carry a cross?"
That question changes everything.

Because somewhere in our generation, many men have learned how to impress people but have never learned how to surrender to God. They know how to pursue promotions, possessions, platforms, and pleasure, but they have never truly discovered what the Lord seeks in a husband.
And that matters because marriage was never created primarily to make us happy.
It was created to reveal Christ.
The Apostle Paul writes in Ephesians 5:25:
The Greek text uses the phrase:

Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν
(Christos ēgapēsen tēn ekklēsian)
"Christ loved the church."
The word ἠγάπησεν (ēgapēsen) comes from agapaō, the deepest form of sacrificial love. This is not emotional affection. This is covenant love. Cross-bearing love. Bleeding love.
The kind of love that keeps loving when nobody applauds.
The kind of love that remains faithful when feelings fluctuate.
The kind of love that chooses sacrifice over self.
That immediately reveals something astonishing.
God is not first looking for a husband who can lead a woman.
He is looking for a man who can follow Christ.
Because no man can love a wife like Jesus until he first learns how to kneel before Jesus.
Many men want authority.
God looks for humility.
Many men want admiration.
God looks for surrender.
Many men want a wife.
God wants a disciple.
That is why one of the most powerful descriptions of biblical manhood appears long before marriage enters the picture.
In Genesis 2:15, Scripture says:
"The LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it."
The Hebrew says:

לְעָבְדָהּ וּלְשָׁמְרָהּ
(le'ovdah u'leshomrah)
"To serve it and to guard it."
Notice that carefully.
Before Adam was given a wife, he was given responsibility.
Before companionship came stewardship.
Before romance came obedience.
God was establishing a principle that still stands today.
A husband is not first a consumer.
He is a caretaker.
He is not called to ask, "What can I get?"
He is called to ask, "What can I protect, serve, and nurture for God's glory?"
The world teaches men to chase what benefits them.
The Gospel teaches men to become a blessing.
That difference changes marriages.
And perhaps this is where some hearts begin to ache.
Because if we're honest, many men can look back at seasons of selfishness.
Moments they should have listened but didn't.
Moments they should have prayed but didn't.
Moments they should have protected but didn't.
Moments they should have loved but didn't.
The enemy loves using those memories to whisper condemnation.
But the Gospel tells a different story.
The Bible is full of deeply flawed men.
Abraham lied.
Jacob deceived.
Moses doubted.
David committed adultery.
Peter denied Christ.
Yet Jesus rewrote their stories.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Not perfection.
Redemption.
Not flawless performance.
Transforming grace.
This is why the cross remains the center of everything.
When Jesus cried out in Aramaic:

"אֱלָהִי אֱלָהִי לְמָה שְׁבַקְתַּנִי"
(Elohi, Elohi, lama shbaqtani)
"My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?"
He was bearing the judgment sinners deserved.
Including every failed husband.
Every selfish husband.
Every absent husband.
Every broken husband.
Every man who looks at his life and wishes he could rewrite entire chapters.
The beautiful truth is that Jesus specializes in rewriting chapters.
That is what grace does.
A man's past may explain him.
But it does not have to define him.
The cross is God's declaration that your worst moment does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
And when Christ transforms a man, something extraordinary begins happening.
He becomes safe.
Not perfect.
Safe.
His wife knows she can trust him.
His children know they can follow him.
His friends know they can depend on him.
His church knows he serves faithfully.
His community sees integrity.
Not because he is sinless.
But because he is submitted.
That is one of the greatest misunderstandings in modern culture.
Strength is often defined by domination.
The Kingdom defines strength through submission to God.
The strongest man in a room is often the one most surrendered to Christ.
Jesus Himself demonstrated this.
Philippians 2 tells us that though He was God, He humbled Himself.
The King became a servant.
The Creator washed feet.
The Lion became the Lamb.
And that is exactly why Godly husbands resemble Christ.
They are leaders who serve.
Protectors who sacrifice.
Providers who trust God.
Men who understand that biblical leadership is not demanding others carry your burdens.
It is willingly carrying burdens for others.
A husband who loves like Christ does not ask, "How much can I get away with?"
He asks, "How much can I give?"
He does not weaponize Scripture.
He embodies Scripture.
He does not quote Ephesians 5 to demand submission.
He reads Ephesians 5 and falls to his knees because he realizes the impossible standard Christ has set before him.
Love her like Jesus loved the Church.
Die to yourself.
Serve faithfully.
Remain loyal.
Lead spiritually.
Protect sacrificially.
Forgive generously.
Stand courageously.
That kind of love changes homes.
And maybe while reading this, someone feels convicted.
Not condemned.
Convicted.
There is a difference.
Condemnation says:
"You are too far gone."
Conviction says:
"Come back home."
One comes from the enemy.
The other comes from the Holy Spirit.
If God is revealing areas that need surrender, that is evidence of His love.
Because the Lord disciplines those He loves.
He is not exposing wounds to shame you.
He is exposing them to heal you.
Perhaps you are a husband carrying regrets.
Perhaps you are a future husband wondering if you will ever measure up.
Perhaps you are a wife praying for your husband.
Perhaps you are a single woman asking God for wisdom about the kind of man you should marry.
Hear this clearly.
God is not looking for a perfect husband.
He is looking for a surrendered one.
A man whose heart echoes the words of Jesus in Gethsemane:
"Not my will, but thine, be done."
The Greek text says:

μὴ τὸ θέλημά μου ἀλλὰ τὸ σὸν γινέσθω
(mē to thelēma mou alla to son ginesthō)
"Not my will, but Yours be done."
That may be the most important prayer any husband can ever pray.
Because every great marriage is ultimately built by people who have learned how to surrender.
And surrender always leads to transformation.
That is why the Gospel remains humanity's greatest love story.
Jesus saw us at our worst.
Loved us anyway.
Pursued us anyway.
Redeemed us anyway.
And through His grace, rewrote everything.
Maybe that is exactly what someone reading this needs to hear today.
Your story is not over.
Your failures are not final.
Your mistakes are not your identity.
Your scars are not your destiny.
Jesus is still rewriting lives.
Jesus is still restoring marriages.
Jesus is still rebuilding families.
Jesus is still transforming husbands.
Jesus is still making all things new.

One day every title, paycheck, achievement, possession, and earthly accomplishment will fade away—but the man who learned to love like Christ will leave fingerprints of eternity on every life he touched.
